source.title: MegDet: A Large Mini-Batch Object Detector
source.authors: Chao Peng; Te-Te Xiao; Ze-Ming Li; Yu-Ning Jiang; Xiangyu Zhang; Kai Jia; Gang Yu; Jian Sun

record.file_problem: The supplied text contains the full paper; some table layout is flattened, but the reported values remain assignable.
record.tranche_reason: Tests large-batch training in object detection, a new setting for the generalization-gap claim, and reports validation accuracy under varied batch sizes and training recipes.
record.gate_note: The paper reports COCO validation mmAP for batch-size, batch-normalization, GPU-count, and training-policy conditions. The cited results from other papers are not extracted as rows.
record.test_reason: Tests V5 in a new workload: COCO object detection. Batch-size sweeps compare held-out mmAP under fixed 11- or 18-epoch budgets, with learning-rate scaling, warmup and normalization changes.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is accurate: warmup plus Cross-GPU Batch Normalization enables large-batch detector training with maintained or improved validation accuracy and substantially shorter training time. The experiments also show that warmup alone is insufficient for the larger batches.
record.recipe_differences: Object detection on COCO with ResNet-50/FPN; adds warmup and Cross-GPU Batch Normalization to support large mini-batches. Reports validation mmAP rather than an explicit train-test error gap.
record.method_sensitivity: Outcome varies with batch size, BN statistics batch size, learning rate, and normal versus long training policy.
record.peer_reviewed: 2018 IEEE/CVF Conference on Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition
record.problems: No training-error values or explicit train-test gaps are reported, so validation mmAP only indirectly bears on the generalization-gap version. The reported results are for one backbone and one detection dataset; no uncertainty estimates are given.
record.rows_left_out: No eligible reported validation mmAP results from Tables 2 or 3 were left out.

untested.parts: Random-label fitting and its coexistence with natural-label generalization.
Width sweeps beyond the interpolation threshold.
Convolutional versus fully connected architectures and local connectivity.
Adaptive versus SGD optimizer comparisons and tuning budgets.
Image classification and language modeling directly; batch sizes beyond 256; explicit training-versus-test gaps; separating the individual contributions of warmup and learning-rate scaling.
Dropout effects and interactions with training-set size, augmentation and weight decay.
Magnitude-aware sharpness and its correlation with generalization gaps.
Removal of memorized examples versus random examples.

missing.what: Batch 16 with BN size 2 on eight GPUs reaches 31.0 mmAP. This normalization control helps distinguish insufficient BN statistics from optimization batch-size effects.
Batch 128 with BN size 16 on 64 GPUs reaches 37.0 mmAP under the normal policy, preserving accuracy relative to batch 16 with the same BN size.
Batch 256 with BN size 16 on 128 GPUs reaches 37.7 mmAP under the long policy. This is the matched-normalization comparator to R17 and the experiment underlying Figure 4.
Batch 32 without trainable BN sometimes fails despite warmup; the successful 36.4-mmAP run does not capture this instability.

record.verdict_notes: Object detection extends V5's workload scope. Held-out mmAP directly tests its performance component, although no explicit train-test gap is reported. Convergence failures do not establish a generalization penalty. Table 3 contains several extraction misalignments; matched-normalization comparisons are preferable to the fixed-BN 16-base reference. No uncertainty estimates are supplied, and this study is not an original source for V5.

versions.untested_parts: Random-label memorization and natural-label generalization coexistence.
Network width beyond interpolation and test-error trends.
Convolutional versus fully connected architecture comparisons.
Language models, workload-dependent batch thresholds, and explicit training-error measurements of the generalization gap.
Dropout and its interactions with augmentation and weight decay.
Sharpness measures and their relation to train-test gaps.
Removing memorized training examples and measuring resulting test accuracy.
